title: Emma Lazarus
hookLine: her poem on the Statue of Liberty welcomes the tired and the poor

lines: GIVE ME YOUR TIRED, YOUR POOR.
PUT UP AFTER SHE WAS GONE.
cards: "Give me your tired, your poor." Those words hang on a plaque at the Statue of Liberty. They weren't there when the statue went up.
A young poet in New York wrote them for a fundraiser, to help pay for the statue's pedestal. After the fundraiser, the poem was set aside. She died before anyone put it on the plaque.
Today, the woman who gave a silent statue its voice. Her name was Emma Lazarus.

teach.h: A POET FROM AN OLD FAMILY.
teach.b: Emma Lazarus did not come over in the great wave.
She came from a Sephardi family long settled in New York, comfortable and educated, with roots in the congregation from three days ago, the one that traces its beginning to the refugees from Brazil.
She read widely and wrote poems from a young age.
Then refugees from the pogroms began arriving at the docks. She is remembered for going to meet them, working with the newcomers, and writing about Jewish life and Jewish dignity with a new fire.
Then came the poem, a sonnet called "The New Colossus." The old Colossus was a giant bronze statue of the ancient Greek world.
Her poem opens with what the new statue is not: "Not like the brazen giant of Greek fame, With conquering limbs astride from land to land."
Instead, a woman with a torch stands at the gate, and her name is "Mother of Exiles." A giant built for welcome instead of conquest.
Then the statue speaks, with silent lips: "Give me your tired, your poor, Your huddled masses yearning to breathe free."

teach.h: YE KNOW THE HEART OF A STRANGER.
teach.b: The Torah gives a reason for that kind of welcome, a reason from memory: "ye know the heart of a stranger, seeing ye were strangers in the land of Egypt."

You've been the stranger, so you know how it feels from the inside. A Jewish poet from an old family looked at strangers stepping off the boat with nothing, and wrote words that let the statue say: I know your heart.

how: Jewish communities and teachers sometimes read Emma Lazarus's sonnet beside the Torah's command about the stranger, and Jewish refugee and immigrant aid groups draw on both.

games.q: you're a poet asked to write for a fundraiser for a giant statue's pedestal. what do you make the statue say?
o: a boast about the country's power.
a welcome to the tired, the poor and the exiled.
games.why: her statue speaks with silent lips: "give me your tired, your poor." a giant built for welcome, not conquest.

practice: Say the poem's name for the statue once, quietly: Mother of Exiles. Then think of a door you hold in your own life, your table, a group, a conversation, and who is standing just outside it, not quite sure they may come in.
Picture the torch held up, not a fist.

wordCard.voice: Emma Lazarus. The New York poet whose sonnet gave the Statue of Liberty its voice of welcome: Mother of Exiles. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the stranger, someone living among a people not their own, the word in Exodus 23:9.

carryVoice: Your line: the new colossus. Strength that welcomes, instead of standing over people. See you next time.
